q: What is the purpose of the Dear Colleague Letter re: New IRB Application Forms and IRB Training Requirement of 9/06?
title: Dear Colleague Letter re: New IRB Application Forms and IRB Training Requirement of 9/06
answer:
According to the Dear Colleague Letter re: New IRB Application Forms and IRB Training Requirement of 9/06: Dear Research Colleagues, RE: New IRB application forms and IRB training requirement. During this last year, the IRB approved new IRB application forms to replace those used previously. The primary goal in the revision process was to assist researchers in providing the detailed information required for IRB approval and to reduce the number of revisions required.
Source: https://www.csulb.edu/sites/default/files/document/dear_colleague_letter_re_new_irb_application_forms_and_irb_training_requirement_of_9_06.pdf
passage:
Published by: the CSULB Office of Research and Economic Development
Dear Research Colleagues,

RE: New IRB application forms and IRB training requirement.
During this last year, the IRB approved new IRB application forms to replace those used previously. The primary goal in the revision process was to assist researchers in providing the detailed information required for IRB approval and to reduce the number of revisions required.
More specific information has been provided on the fonns and, in some cases, check boxes have been used to simplify the responses from IRB applicants. The two new fom1s are posted as items P and Q on the IRB website:
http://www.csulb.edu/divisions/aa/research/our/compliance/irb/ The forms have been posted and used since March 2006. One form is for use when the proposed research utilizes existing data. The other form is for use for all other IRB applications:
administrative review, expedited review, and standard review. Because some of you may have "legacy" versions of the previous IRB application forms stored on your computer, it is important to delete these older versions and download the new forms as soon as possible. Beginning September 12, 2006, the IRB will not accept applications unless the new form is utilized.

q: Give me an overview of the CSULB Dear Campus Community Letter re: Introducing IRBNet of 4/20/12.
title: Dear Campus Community Letter re: Introducing IRBNet of 4/20/12
answer:
According to the Dear Campus Community Letter re: Introducing IRBNet of 4/20/12: TO: The Campus Community FROM: Al Russo, Director of Research Compliance Office of Research & Sponsored Programs (ORSP) SUBJECT: Introducing IRBNet The Office of Research & Sponsored Programs (ORSP) is pleased to announce the adoption of the industry leading IRBNet suite of tools, bringing electronic protocol management, on-line submissions and many other important features to the CSULB research community.
Source: https://www.csulb.edu/sites/default/files/document/dear_campus_community_letter_re_introducing_irbnet_of_4_20_12.pdf
passage:
Published by: the CSULB Office of Research and Economic Development
TO:

The Campus Community

FROM: Al Russo, Director of Research Compliance Office of Research & Sponsored Programs (ORSP)

SUBJECT: Introducing IRBNet The Office of Research & Sponsored Programs (ORSP) is pleased to announce the adoption of the industry leading IRBNet suite of tools, bringing electronic protocol management, on-line submissions and many other important features to the CSULB research community. ORSP and the CSULB research community have long recognized the need to reduce manual and paper-based procedures, streamline protocol submission and review processes and leverage today's best technologies throughout the research lifecycle. As an important step toward these objectives, ORSP's adoption of IRBNet now brings the CSULB community a robust set of electronic tools supporting the management, submission, review and oversight of our research protocols. Some of IRBNet's many features include electronic document management, web-based protocol sharing and collaboration, automatic notifications, electronic submissions and reviews, and important audit capabilities including electronic revision histories, electronic signatures and event tracking.
ORSP has carefully chosen IRBNet not only for the important capabilities that it provides, but also because IRBNet is secure, web-based, and extremely intuitive and easy to use. You may access IRBNet from virtually any computer using a web browser by visiting www.irbnet.org.
Training Sessions will be offered in the ORSP Seminar Room (F05-116) on the following dates. Each session should last less than an hour.

q: The Importance of Preserving Evidence - what are the rules at CSULB?
title: Title IX Resources Handbook
answer:
According to the Title IX Resources Handbook, section "The Importance of Preserving Evidence": It is important that you take steps to preserve and collect evidence; doing so preserves the full range of options available to you, be it through the University's administrative complaint procedures or criminal prosecution.
Source: https://www.csulb.edu/sites/default/files/2026/documents/OEC%20-%20Title%20IX%20Campus%20Resources%20Booklet_7.%202026.pdf

It is important that you take steps to preserve and collect evidence; doing so preserves the full range of options available to you, be it through the University's administrative complaint procedures or criminal prosecution. To preserve evidence: (1) do not Wash your face or hands;
(2) do not shower or bathe; (3) do not brush your teeth; (4) do not change clothes or straighten up the area where the assault took place; (5) do not dispose of clothes or other items that were present during the assault, or use the restroom; and, (6) seek a medical exam immediately. If you already cleaned up from the assault, you can still report the crime, as well as seek medical or counseling treatment. You should preserve text messages, social media postings, or notes that demonstrate the course of conduct. Contemporaneous photos of bruises or other injuries are helpful. WHAT REPORTING OPTIONS DO I HAVE?
The University's primary concern is your safety and the safety of the campus community. The use of alcohol or drugs never makes the victim at fault for sexual misconduct/sexual assault.

B. Employees Who Do Not Have a Duty to Report: Except as required by law (described in section C), the Employees identified below generally do not have a duty to report to the Title IX Coordinator/DHR Administrator.

-

The website substantially conforms with Level A and Level AA of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) version 2.1.

answer:

Content creators and other roles can review basic accessibility feedback with automatic testing tools like WAVE.

The WAVE Web Accessibility Evaluation Tool by Web Accessibility in Mind (WebAIM) is also an automated accessibility tool. WAVE helps content editors make their web content more accessible. The WAVE tool can be added as an extension to most browsers. The extension can check password-protected, dynamically generated, or sensitive web pages. The WAVE extension evaluates the rendered version of your page, locally displayed styles and dynamically generated content from scripts.

Note: Once the WAVE tool has run, it can be helpful to uncheck the ARIA checkbox. The Drupal templates use ARIA and it can be confusing to see all the ARIA icons and associated text. ARIA is included at the template level and is reviewed regularly to ensure accessibility issues are not introduced.

q: What does the CSULB Web Accessibility say about manual testing?
title: Web Accessibility
answer:
According to the Web Accessibility, section "Manual Testing": If your content is not on the primary CSULB web presences, it must be manually reviewed for accessibility. Accessibility review will check template pages to identify sitewide issues, then the content will be added to our institutional accessibility tool of record and a quarterly accessibility report will be provided.
Source: https://www.csulb.edu/information-technology/accessible-technology/web-accessibility
heading: Manual Testing
passage:
If your content is not on the primary CSULB web presences, it must be manually reviewed for accessibility. Accessibility review will check template pages to identify sitewide issues, then the content will be added to our institutional accessibility tool of record and a quarterly accessibility report will be provided. Please request a manual review through Accessibility Support.

CSULB websites using standard templates (Canvas, Drupal and a few other) are not required to go through manual testing, though the expectation is they are following the Accessibility Best Practices. If you would like feedback, request it through Accessibility Support.

Manual testing involves testing with assistive technology and expert experience to ensure users have access to content regardless of disability. This testing has multiple steps, though the primary tests performed are:

- Keyboard navigation "Tab test" - Use the Keyboard to navigate through content to ensure all functionality is accessible to someone using switch or other alternative devices

- Assistive Technology Review - Depending on content, a review of the accessibility tree or review using Assistive Technology such as a screen reader to review the content may be warranted.

- Enlargement and Reflow test - Setting the appropriate viewport size and enlargement to test Success Criterion 1.4.10: Reflow and Success Criterion 1.4.4: Resize Text

q: What is the CSULB policy on manual testing?
title: Web Accessibility
answer:
According to the Web Accessibility, section "Manual Testing": - Common Code issues - Aided by automated testing tools like WAVE, we review content to ensure it does not have common design or developer issues like pseudo-headings, tables are designed properly and other HELPS Structural issues. ; Color Contrast test - review colors used to ensure it meets color contrast and other HELPS Presentation recommendations. ; Video, audio, and image review - review audio and visual content for compliance with relevant requirements.
Source: https://www.csulb.edu/information-technology/accessible-technology/web-accessibility
heading: Manual Testing
passage:
- Common Code issues - Aided by automated testing tools like WAVE, we review content to ensure it does not have common design or developer issues like pseudo-headings, tables are designed properly and other HELPS Structural issues.

- Color Contrast test - review colors used to ensure it meets color contrast and other HELPS Presentation recommendations.

- Video, audio, and image review - review audio and visual content for compliance with relevant requirements. See HELPS Explain Audio and Visual Content for examples we look for.

- Content Review - Feedback is provided on content to ensure that it is accessible. This covers best practices identified mostly in HELPS Language and HELPS Headings.

Alternative text or alt text is the mechanism to provide screen reader users with a text replacement of an image. Alt text is also read by search engines and audio only devices, making graphical content discoverable by search engines and usable on screen optional devices.

Even though the automatic accessibility tool will check to see if an image has alt text, it is up to the developer or content editor to make sure the alt attribute is a meaningful replacement.

The simplest way to review your alt text is using the WAVE tool. The alt text will be presented under each image on your web page.

q: What is the CSULB policy on guidelines for alternative text?
title: Web Accessibility
answer:
According to the Web Accessibility, section "Guidelines for Alternative Text": - Alt text can be as long as necessary, but brevity is preferred. If the alt text you would use is duplicated in text, or the image is unimportant to the context of the page, it can be marked as "decorative image". In Drupal 7, you can use the null string, which is a pair of double quotes with nothing between them: "". ; Alt text should be succinct.
Source: https://www.csulb.edu/information-technology/accessible-technology/web-accessibility

In Drupal 7, you can use the null string, which is a pair of double quotes with nothing between them: "".

- Alt text should be succinct. Correct sentence and grammatic structure is unnecessary. Unless your audience is interpreting an image, 2-3 words are often sufficient.

- Alt text should be accurate and equivalent to the visual content. There is no maximum length on alt text. It is best to minimize description in alt text and cover the most important information first. Making the description part of the main page content is helpful for people not using screen readers.

- Alt text should never be left as the filename, even if the filename is otherwise the same as your alt text (ex. "LBS_Financial Credit_Union_Pyramid.jpg" should be changed to "LBS Financial Credit Union Pyramid").

- If the image contains text, the alt text should contain the same text, unless the text is unimportant (ex: signs out of focus but visible in the background) or included as text on the same page or a linked page.

- If the image is used as a link, it should provide information about the linked content. Example alt="CSU Long Beach" for the logo linked to the main home page.

- Alt text should not include "image of", "link", or any other similar descriptive text.
